fd is a filename finder, and it does not pretend otherwise. Nothing in src/ reads file contents — there is no content-search module — so greping inside files is out of scope by design; pair fd with a content tool, which is exactly the division of labor between fd and ripgrep. Consequences follow from that scope: a pattern containing / cannot match a bare file name, so fd raises a friendly error suggesting --full-path instead of silently returning nothing (main.rs, L176).

Default behavior has sharp edges worth knowing. Ignore rules apply only inside git repositories unless you pass --no-require-git (cli.rs, L96); hidden files mean only leading-dot names (cli.rs, L40) — macOS’s resource forks or Windows system attributes are not “hidden” to fd; and smart case is evaluated per-pattern, with fixed/exact strings falling back to a plain uppercase scan (patterns.rs, L118). Platform quirks are documented in the tree: --list-details shells out to ls and errors on Windows without GNU ls installed (main.rs, L453), and the jemalloc allocator is compiled out on macOS and Windows entirely (Cargo.toml, L66). None of these are bugs — they are the cost of the single-crate, do-one-thing design that makes the source above worth reading in an afternoon.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of fd: how the ignore crate's parallel WalkBuilder, a cheap-first filter chain, gitignore handling and a 100 ms output buffer make fd so fast.

entry.title: Inside the fish Shell: How Typed Characters Become Running Jobs

link.title: Inside the fish Shell: How Typed Characters Become Running Jobs

entry.content:
Open fish for the first time, type git che, and a gray ghost of a full command appears at the end of your line — a real suggestion pulled from your history, not a canned prefix. Press the right-arrow key and it lands in your buffer. No plugin manager, no ~/.fishrc incantation, no four-hour rabbit hole. That “it just works” feeling is the surface of a very deep machine, and the machine is worth opening.

The moment you press Enter, that friendly line editor transforms into something closer to a compiler backend: the buffer is tokenized, parsed into a typed tree, expanded through five distinct stages, packaged into a Job of Process structs, assigned a process group, and handed to posix_spawn or fork. A piped command like grep error log/**.log | wc -l is not “run” — it is assembled, piece by piece, from data structures fish has been mutating since before you finished typing.

One more reason this tour is timely: fish was famously a C++ codebase for two decades, but fish 4.0 ported the core to Rust (the changelog tracks it as issue #9512). Today’s master contains no C++ sources at all — just Rust crates, a workspace Cargo.toml declaring version 4.9.3, and the Rust 1.85 MSRV. Reading the source now means reading Rust.

The whole journey at a glance: the interactive reader on the left feeds the parser, expansion turns strings into candidates, and the execution layer turns the AST into real processes — all backed by layered shell state.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Startup is tiny. The binary entry point main, L349 parses flags, decides whether the session is interactive, and calls reader_read, L549 on stdin. Everything users associate with fish — prompt, suggestions, colors — hangs off that single call.
  • The reader parses while you type, not just after Enter. read_i builds a config with syntax_check_ok: true (read_i, L824), so the buffer is continuously parsed for live highlighting and error marking — the dashed edge from the reader back into the parse tree in the diagram.
  • One parse function serves everything. Interactive evaluation, fish -c, config files, and even the highlighter all funnel through parse_source, L257, which calls ast::parse, L1400 to build a JobList tree and wraps it in a ParsedSource, L109 that keeps the original string alive for source ranges.
  • Expansion is a stage machine, not a regex soup. expand_string, L201 drives separate stages for tilde, variables, braces, command substitution, and wildcards — each stage can multiply the candidate list.
  • A Job is built before anything runs. run_1_job, L1546 creates the job object (Job::new, L1665) and only then calls exec_job, L1695. Construction and execution are cleanly separated.
  • Process groups are a first-class concept. Every job carries a JobGroup, L59 holding the pgid, terminal-ownership flags, and a cancel signal — this is what makes Ctrl-C hit the whole piped command and not fish itself.
  • Universal state sits at the bottom of the stack. EnvStack, L212 layers variable scopes; the EnvUniversal, L41 database feeds the universal layer, which is why set -U survives restarts and crosses fish instances.

The detail view: each group in the overview unpacks into the real modules — the readline event loop, the parse tree, the five expansion stages, the spawn path, and the state stores.

Tokenize, Parse, and the Rust AST

Fish’s grammar is unusual among shells because it is typed rather than ad hoc, and the Rust rewrite doubled down on that. The Tokenizer, L238 first turns raw source into a flat stream of TokenType, L18 values — strings, pipes, redirections, ends — handling quoting and escape rules that date back two decades.

Then the interesting part happens. Instead of an interpreter wandering over tokens, ast::parse, L1400 runs a Populator that directly fills Rust structs: a JobPipeline, L767 is one chain of piped commands, AndorJob, L1007 captures and/or chaining, and a DecoratedStatement, L954 is one command with its sudo-style decorators. The result is a strongly-typed tree rooted at JobList (Ast, L1445) — there is no void * node soup, so the compiler itself rejects malformed tree walks.

The Parser, L390 then does evaluation. Its eval_with, L524 parses the string and hands the tree to eval_node, L630, which constructs an ExecutionContext, L119 and dispatches: job lists to run_job_list, L1795, if/while/for to their dedicated run_* methods. Syntax errors are therefore impossible past this point — the doc comment on eval_parsed_source, L561 says exactly that: “Because the source has been parsed, a syntax error is impossible.”

Expansion: Five Stages Before Anything Runs

A fish argument like ~/$project/*.{rs,toml} is not a string — it is a plan that explodes into dozens of real arguments. The expansion layer implements that plan as an ordered stage machine inside expand.rs: stage_cmdsubst, L1389, stage_variables, L1436, stage_braces, L1476, home-directory expansion at stage_home_and_self, L1480, and finally stage_wildcards, L1497.

The stages are honest about their jobs. expand_tilde, L348 consults the environment for $HOME and ~user. expand_variables, L608 implements fish’s signature list semantics — one variable can expand to many arguments, with slices like $list[1..3]. expand_braces, L845 does the Cartesian product. Command substitution (expand_cmdsubst, L969) is special because it must execute code, so it calls into the execution layer — you can see the edge from expansion to exec_subshell_for_expand in the detail diagram.

Wildcards get their own module because they are the only stage that touches the filesystem. wildcard_expand_string, L1021 walks directory trees to materialize matches for * and the recursive **, while wildcard_match, L1078 does the filtering and wildcard_has, L1165 decides whether a string is a glob at all. If you like this layer, the fast path-friendly sibling tool in this series — ripgrep for searching — solves adjacent problems with the same rigor.

From a Job to a Living Process

Execution begins as bookkeeping. run_1_job, L1546 checks --no-execute, records the executing node for profiling, and applies per-job variable assignments before Job::new, L1665 assembles a Job, L613 — a sequence of Process, L365 structs, each tagged with a ProcessType, L55 of external, builtin, function, or block. Only when the whole job is described does exec_job, L86 start it.

exec_job is where the pipe plumbing lives. Its comment explains that up to three pipes can be “in flight” — the one to read from, the one to write to, and the one for the next process — and the loop over processes wires them up, passing each to exec_process_in_job, L1222. That dispatcher routes to exec_builtin_process, L1187 for builtins and exec_block_or_func_process, L1054 for functions, both of which run inside the fish process, recursively re-entering the parser.

External commands take the spawn path. exec_external_command, L861 builds argv/envv, computes a PgroupPolicy (lead a new group, join the job’s pgid, or inherit fish’s), and prefers posix_spawn via PosixSpawner, L96 because it is faster than fork on systems like macOS; otherwise fork_child_for_process, L692 takes over. Meanwhile the JobGroup, L59 tracks whether the job wants the terminal and who is foreground, so job control — suspending, resuming, Ctrl-C — behaves. Finished jobs are collected by job_reap, L983, and wait waits through proc_wait_any, L1115. The pairing of a shell with a fast terminal emulator — alacritty, for instance — only matters because fish is this careful about who owns the tty.

The Reader: Autosuggestions and Highlighting

The interactive layer is the part you actually see. The event loop is Reader::readline, L2570: it consumes CharEvents, applies key bindings resolved through BindingSet, L298, and repaints the screen. Every edit triggers update_autosuggestion, L5591, which asks the persistent History, L1191 store for a matching prefix and then validates it — autosuggest_validate_from_history, L355 re-runs the suggestion through the highlighter to avoid proposing commands that would fail. Pressing right-arrow calls accept_autosuggestion, L5670. Tab completions flow from complete, L2534 into the Pager, L90, and the coloring itself is produced by highlight_shell, L96, which is why invalid commands turn red before you press Enter. If you enjoy that interactive-selection workflow, fzf composes beautifully with fish’s history pager, and starship plugs into the same prompt-event hook fish exposes.

Universal Variables: State That Follows You

set -U EDITOR vim works across every open fish and every future fish. The keeper of that promise is EnvUniversal, L41, which tracks modified keys in a dirty set and writes them via sync, L162 to a single file resolved by default_vars_path, L627 — the fish_variables file in your config directory. Cross-instance awareness comes from a small family of notifier backends; on Linux the notifyd-based NotifydNotifier, L28 watches that file so a second fish session picks up changes without polling. Exported universal variables additionally bump an export generation count, visible right in the struct’s fields.

From Cargo Build to First Prompt

Building fish from source is a standard Rust workflow wrapped in a thin CMake shell, and the README, L116 states the requirements plainly: Rust 1.85 or later with cargo, CMake 3.15+, a C compiler for feature detection, and a network connection since dependencies download automatically. The canonical install path (README, L140) is:

mkdir build; cd build
cmake ..
cmake --build .
sudo cmake --install .

CMake exists because fish needs system feature detection, but underneath it drives cargo: the workspace root Cargo.toml declares the fish binary at src/bin/fish.rs, alongside fish_indent and fish_key_reader, and pins the workspace to edition 2024. The compiled binary needs no runtime interpreter — the AST machinery above is compiled in.

Honest Limits

Fish’s friendliness is a deliberate trade, documented rather than hidden. The design document lists POSIX conformance only as its third goal, to be followed “whenever possible without breaking the above goals” (design.rst, L10), and the bash-migration doc opens with the blunter sentence: “fish is intentionally not POSIX-compatible” (fish_for_bash_users.rst, L4). Practically: variables never word-split, there are no heredocs, string manipulation replaces ${foo%bar}, and only * and ** are glob syntax — a non-matching glob fails the command rather than passing a literal * (fish_for_bash_users.rst, L114). Scripts written for sh/bash need porting; fish is not a drop-in /bin/sh replacement. The Rust port is real but young by shell standards — the C++ era left twenty years of optimization history, and the port notes in the changelog are candid that packaging and build dependencies changed wholesale. None of this is instability so much as a stated identity: fish optimizes for the interactive human first, and the source makes that choice visible at every layer.
entry.summary: A source tour of the fish shell's Rust rewrite: the parser, expansion stages, job groups, universal variables, and the reader that make fish feel magic.

entry.title: Inside fzf: The Fuzzy Matching Architecture Behind Instant Interactive Search

link.title: Inside fzf: The Fuzzy Matching Architecture Behind Instant Interactive Search

entry.content:
Type three characters into fzf while a million lines stream through it, and the best match appears before your finger leaves the key. That is not a shortcut: every keystroke triggers a full pass over every candidate, scoring each one against the query. A typical shell history of 100,000 entries, or a recursive file walk over half a million paths, gets re-ranked from scratch, repeatedly, at human typing speed. Most tools fake this by throttling input or building indexes up front; fzf does neither.

The trick is that nothing in the design is slow enough to need faking. Input arrives in fixed-size chunks that can be matched independently, matching is spread across every CPU core, each core reuses pre-allocated memory arenas so the garbage collector never stalls the loop, and the final ranking compresses into a single 64-bit integer comparison per item. The result is a flow with no stage slower than the one before it, so the perceived latency is just the sum of a few cheap passes.

So what actually happens between the moment fzf starts and the instant the first keystroke produces a ranked list? In this post we walk the Go source of junegunn/fzf and trace the whole journey: the concurrent reader, the chunked store, the scoring algorithm behind the fuzziness, the parallel matcher, and the terminal loop that ties it together. The two diagrams below are generated directly from the repository tree.

The fzf architecture as five collaborating components. Everything left of the matcher runs continuously in the background; everything right of it reacts to your keystrokes. Click any node to open the exact source file on GitHub.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything is coordinated through one event box. The entire runtime is documented in a comment block: the reader pushes EvtReadNew, the terminal pushes EvtSearchNew, the matcher answers with EvtSearchProgress and EvtSearchFin — see core.go, L16. The coordinator wakes, reacts, and then sleeps on a back-off that grows from 10 ms to a 100 ms ceiling, which is how bursts of keystrokes get batched into fewer searches — core.go, L635.
  • The reader never blocks matching. Run spawns the reader and matcher as bare goroutines around a mutex-guarded chunk list: core.go, L204 wires the reader’s pusher straight into ChunkList.Push, core.go, L210 starts ingestion, and core.go, L360 starts the matcher loop before the terminal even exists.
  • Input is chopped into fixed 1024-item chunks. A Chunk is literally a [chunkSize]Item array — constants.go, L40 and chunklist.go, L6. Fixed size is what makes per-chunk caching and work-stealing matching possible later; variable-length lists would break both.
  • Reader→matcher feedback is a CAS on one int. The reader’s poller loop does a compare-and-swap from EvtReadNew to EvtReady before broadcasting into the shared EventBox, and backs its poll interval off from 10 ms toward 50 ms while the stream is quiet — reader.go, L51. No channel storms while a slow command dribbles out bytes.
  • Matching is per-chunk, per-CPU. The matcher sizes its worker pool to runtime.NumCPU() — matcher.go, L61 — and each worker steals chunks off an atomic counter, so adding a core linearly scales the scan — matcher.go, L194.
  • Scores become one machine word. A Result packs the item plus four uint16 ranking slots — result.go, L27 — and on x86 the comparison casts those slots into a single uint64 equality check — result_x86.go, L7. Sorting a million items is then just an O(n) radix pass — result.go, L354.
  • The terminal loop is the only renderer. Keystrokes, repaints, the spinner and the previewer all funnel through a priority-sorted request box inside Terminal.Loop — terminal.go, L6669. Every query change ends up as EvtSearchNew — terminal.go, L8733 — which is the whole user-facing interface to the matcher.

The detail view follows one query byte-for-byte: ingestion paths on top, storage in the middle, the scoring engine and its fast paths below, and ranking plus the terminal loop on the right.

The Scoring Engine: Greedy V1 Versus Optimal V2

The file that gives fzf its character opens with a forty-line essay on its own algorithm. FuzzyMatchV1 finds the first fuzzy occurrence in O(n) with a forward scan, then walks backwards to shrink the matched window; it is fast but provably suboptimal because it never reconsiders an earlier alignment — the trade-off is spelled out at algo.go, L8. FuzzyMatchV2 implements a modified Smith-Waterman dynamic program that examines all occurrences and returns the highest-scoring one, at O(nm) cost when a match exists and O(n) when it does not — algo.go, L23.

V2 runs in four phases. Phase 1 runs a byte-level prefilter, asciiFuzzyIndex, which skips through the text with SIMD-friendly byte searches to find the narrowest window that can contain the pattern — algo.go, L420. Phase 2 computes a bonus per character position and the first DP row — algo.go, L778. Phase 3 fills the score matrix row by row, tracking gap runs and consecutive-match streaks — algo.go, L848. Phase 4 is an optional backtrace that reconstructs the exact matched positions for highlight rendering — algo.go, L920.

The scoring constants are the personality of the tool. A matched character is worth 16 points, opening a gap costs 3 and extending one costs 1, matching at a word boundary or after a slash earns 8 (the bonus is tuned to die out once the gap grows past 8 characters), camelCase humps earn 7, and consecutive streaks earn 4 — all defined together at algo.go, L112. The first pattern character gets its bonus doubled, because what you type first predicts what you want most.

Two fast paths short-circuit the general machinery. A single ASCII character never allocates a matrix; the code jumps occurrence to occurrence and stops early once it hits a boundary bonus — algo.go, L514. A two-character query collapses DP rows zero and one into scalar running state in a single fused pass — algo.go, L562. These are not heuristics: equivalence tests in algo_test.go force the general path and assert identical results, and make fuzz actively fuzzes the fast paths against the reference implementation.

Ranking: A 64-Bit Key and a Radix Sort

fzf ranks by relevance, never by recency — but the nuance is worth unpacking. The --tiebreak criteria compile into a fixed sortCriteria slice that is set once at startup and never changes — result.go, L120. When each match is built, every criterion is folded into one of four uint16 slots: score (inverted so smaller wins), whole-word chunk length, trimmed item length, and begin/end offsets — result.go, L59. The first criterion lands in the most significant slot, so “tiebreak” is really a compound primary key.

On 386/amd64/arm64, compareRanks reads those four slots as one uint64 through an unsafe pointer cast and does a single integer compare — result_x86.go, L7. Every worker sorts its own partial results with a stable LSD radix sort over that key: eight byte-passes, with any all-zero byte position skipped entirely — result.go, L354. Lists under 128 items fall back to a plain comparison sort because setup overhead dominates. The merge across workers is lazy: Merger.mergedGet advances per-list cursors and always emits the smallest remaining rank, so the user can read the first page of results before the whole merge finishes — merger.go, L155.

Where does time fit? Only after acceptance. When you multi-select items, the output order is re-sorted by the moment you picked each one, via byTimeOrder — terminal.go, L500 — so --multi output reflects your intent sequence, not the search ranking. Scheme presets reshape the criteria instead: --scheme=path ranks by score, then pathname, then length — options.go, L1342 — and fzf auto-selects that scheme when stdin is a TTY and it is walking files — options.go, L3952.

One Million Lines Without a Stutter

Ingestion is deliberately boring. The reader scans a reusable 128 KB slab, splits on newlines (or NUL bytes with --read0), and pushes each record — reader buffers and slab sizes are constants at constants.go, L16, and the split loop is reader.go, L153. With stdin a TTY and no FZF_DEFAULT_COMMAND, fzf instead walks directories in parallel through the fastwalk library — reader.go, L270. A single mutex guards the chunk list; the writer appends chunks while matchers work only on immutable snapshots, duplicated at the boundary so a mid-chunk append can never race a scan — chunklist.go, L118.

The real anti-stutter weapon is caching at two granularities. Per chunk, matching indexes are stored as bitmaps keyed by query string, and on a miss the cache hands back the longest cached prefix or suffix of the current query, so typing “foob” after “foo” only diffs the last character — cache.go, L72. Whole results are memoized too: an unchanged item count plus a repeat query returns the previous merger outright — matcher.go, L126. Both caches refuse low-selectivity queries: chunks with more than 512 matches are never bitmap-cached and mergers above 100,000 matches are never memoized — constants.go, L48.

Pattern parsing is its own mini-language: ^prefix, suffix$, 'exact, !inverse, "quoted exact", and | for OR-groups, all parsed into term sets that AND across sets and OR within — pattern.go, L168. The common case gets a dedicated bypass: a single non-inverse fuzzy term calls the algorithm function directly, skipping the generic term machinery — pattern.go, L340. Even memory churn is engineered away: every match scratch buffer comes from per-worker Slab arenas of pre-allocated int16/int32 slices, sized once — slab.go, L8 and constants.go, L44 — so steady-state searching performs close to zero allocations. It is the same allocation discipline you see in other hot Go tools like ripgrep’s mmap-heavy search loop, and it pairs beautifully with pipe sources such as fd — fd | fzf is the canonical combo — or with git output for interactive branch and stash pickers.

From Make Build to First Search

The build is refreshingly plain. BUILD.md requires only Go 1.23 or newer; make builds a binary for your platform into target/, and make install copies it to bin/ — the targets live at Makefile, L88 and Makefile, L126. The Makefile detects your architecture via uname and stamps version and revision into the binary through -ldflags "-X main.version=..." — Makefile, L37. make build hands off to goreleaser for all-platform archives — Makefile, L131.

The module is nearly dependency-free: go.mod pulls in tcell for fullscreen TUI, fastwalk for the directory walker, uniseg for Unicode segmentation, and a handful of terminal helpers. Entry is main.go, which embeds the shell key-binding scripts and man page into the binary via go:embed and then calls fzf.Run(options) — main.go, L113. From there, the pieces you now know assemble in one function: chunk list, terminal, reader goroutine, matcher loop, coordinator. The first keystroke you type lands in a system that has already been ingesting data the whole time.

Honest Limits

fzf is fast, but the source is candid about trade-offs. V2’s optimality has a cap: when the product of text and pattern length exceeds the slab capacity, or the pattern runs past 1000 runes, fzf silently falls back to greedy V1 — algo.go, L740. Scores accumulate in 16-bit slots, so extreme scores saturate rather than overflow. Queries containing inverse terms or OR-groups are excluded from chunk-scope caching — pattern.go, L115 — and a query with only inverse terms can’t be sorted at all, only filtered. The interactive UI leans on tcell as an optional fullscreen backend chosen at startup — terminal.go, L1017 — while the default LightRenderer hand-parses ANSI escape sequences; and terminal.go itself is a single file of roughly 8,400 lines, a deliberate monolith that contains the previewer, jump mode, and every action in the keymap. None of these are bugs — they are the visible edges of the same obsession: keep every keystroke cheap enough to pay for a million times per second.
entry.summary: How fzf scores a million lines per keystroke: the Smith-Waterman fuzzy matcher, 1024-item chunk storage, CPU-wide parallel search, and the terminal event loop, explained from the Go source.

entry.title: Inside Git Internals: How the Object Model, Packfiles, and Commit Walks Actually Work

link.title: Inside Git Internals: How the Object Model, Packfiles, and Commit Walks Actually Work

entry.content:
Run git status in a huge repository — say the CPython tree after its move to GitHub — and it answers instantly, while some other tools on the same machine take seconds. Run git log in two repos of comparable history and one may finish in a blink while the other churns. Nothing about your files changed; what differs is how git models what is on disk. Git is not a database of diffs or snapshots in the way most people assume — it is a content-addressed filesystem with three fast bookkeeping layers stacked on top, and nearly every command you type is a walk over that filesystem.

The evidence is sitting in .git/objects right now. Open it and you find 256 two-hex-character directories (ab/, c3/, …), each holding small zlib-compressed files named by a 40-character hash. Those files are your files — but not stored per-branch or per-commit. They are stored once, globally, keyed by the hash of their own content. Nothing inside a loose object ever mentions a branch or even a filename. That single design decision explains deduplication, cheap branches, and why git gc matters.

It also explains why clone sizes surprise people. Two repositories with a similar amount of history can unpack to very different sizes on disk, because git does not store history as a fixed format — it recomputes a compressed representation of it at pack time, using delta heuristics that depend on which objects were chosen as compression bases. Understanding git’s internals means understanding that trade-off, and the heuristics live in plain sight in the C source. This post walks the actual implementation: how object ids are computed and looked up, how the index and refs work, how delta compression squeezes a pack, and how a commit walk finds what you asked for.

Git's core as one graph: commands touch the index, write into the object database through odb_write_object_ext, resolve names through refs, decode packfiles on demand, and traverse history through the revision machinery.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • A commit is made by cmd_commit, L1696, whose real work happens in prepare_to_commit, L762: load staged state, run hooks, get a message — then write objects and move refs.
  • Every write goes through odb_write_object_ext, L696, which hashes the content first; if the object already exists, odb_freshen_object, L566 just refreshes its mtime and skips the write entirely.
  • Loose objects land at a path derived from their own hash: odb_loose_path, L60 builds objects/ab/cdef…, with the fanout directory added by fill_loose_path, L46.
  • Naming is its own subsystem: repo_get_oid, L1538 accepts hex, ref names, @{…} expressions and :path forms via get_oid_basic, L667, while repo_find_unique_abbrev_r, L585 computes the shortest prefix that stays unambiguous.
  • Refs are resolved symbolically by refs_resolve_ref_unsafe, L2136, which follows HEAD → refs/heads/master → an oid, bounded by SYMREF_MAXDEPTH.
  • The index is a single mmapped file, read by do_read_index, L2222 after verify_hdr, L1725 checks the DIRC signature and version.
  • Packed objects are decoded by unpack_entry, L1515, which walks a delta chain back to a real base while paging bytes in through use_pack, L608 — sliding mmap windows, not full-file reads.
  • Walks begin at prepare_revision_walk, L4019, which sorts tips by date, runs limit_list, L1446 to prune excluded ancestors, and applies topological order only when asked.

The detail view: from cmd_commit through hash verification and ref backends, down to delta window search in try_delta and the commit-graph-aware traversal in prepare_revision_walk.

The Object Model: Everything Is a Hash

Git’s four object types — blob, tree, commit, tag — share one storage format. To store an object, git first builds a header of the form <type> <size>\0 in format_object_header, L102, then concatenates it with the payload. The SHA-1 (or SHA-256) of those bytes is the object’s name, and that is why identical files across a million commits share a single blob: the name depends only on content.

What lands on disk is that payload, zlib-compressed, at the fanout path described above. The compression call itself is a plain git_deflate, L784 in the loose-object writer. Reading is the mirror image: check_object_signature, L113 re-hashes the decompressed bytes and compares them to the name the object was fetched under — integrity checking is free because the address is the hash.

Once loaded, every object lives in a typed in-memory representation. parse_object, L398 reads the object, verifies its hash, and dispatches to parse_object_buffer, L261, which understands each type’s grammar — trees as (mode, name, oid) triples, commits as headers plus a message. Nothing is parsed twice if it can be avoided; parsed objects are cached on the repository.

The clever part is lookup. Given git show abc123, git does not need all 40 characters — repo_get_oid, L1538 and get_oid_basic, L667 scan candidates matching the prefix and apply type hints, so an ambiguous abbreviation that could be a commit or a tag prefers the commit via disambiguate_commit_only, L138. The same logic in reverse, repo_find_unique_abbrev_r, L585, is why your short hashes occasionally grow longer: git widens them until they are unique again. The hash family itself is an abstraction (hash.h), so the object database can compute a second, compat hash during writes as visible in odb_write_object_ext, L696.

The Index and Refs: Git’s Fast Layers

The index is not a diff and not a patch — it is a flat, ordered list of (path, mode, oid, stat) records, and it is the only file git status must consult to separate “what changed” from “what is staged”. The format is documented in gitformat-index.adoc: a DIRC magic header, a version, entry count, then entries. Reads are an mmap plus a signature check (do_read_index, L2222, verify_hdr, L1725); writes serialize entries back with path compression in ce_write_entry, L2663, all under a .lock file via write_locked_index, L3384. Each entry records the file’s stat data, which is why status can trust most files without hashing them — and why touching timestamps forces a re-hash.

Refs are even cheaper. A branch is a 41-byte text file containing an oid. refs_resolve_ref_unsafe, L2136 implements the resolution loop: read the raw ref; if it starts with ref: , recurse into the pointed-to name, up to SYMREF_MAXDEPTH — that is how HEAD resolves to your branch to a commit. The generic API sits above swappable backends: the classic files backend reads loose refs and falls through to the mmapped packed-refs file (files_read_raw_ref, L657, packed_read_raw_ref, L835), while the newer reftable backend keeps refs in a log-structured, sorted table (reftable_be_read_raw_ref, L881). Updates go through refs_update_ref, L1579, which verifies the old value before swapping — the foundation of compare-and-swap semantics. Reflogs are written alongside, which is why “deleted” commits stay reachable until expiry.

Packfiles and Delta Compression

Loose objects are for small, recent history. Scale demands compression, and git’s answer is the packfile — a single append-mostly file plus a .idx index, documented in gitformat-pack.adoc. The index maps oid → offset with a binary-searchable table (find_pack_entry_one, L1815); the pack itself stores objects either whole or as deltas against other objects in the same pack.

Two kinds of delta exist: OFS_DELTA, which points backward by offset, and REF_DELTA, which names a base object. Decoding is the job of unpack_entry, L1515: it drills down through delta headers to the innermost base — consulting a small in-memory delta base cache first — then applies deltas on the way back up. Byte access goes through use_pack, L608, which hands out mmap windows and unmaps old ones behind a fixed window count, so reading a 2 GB pack never requires 2 GB of address space.

Packing is where the real money is saved, and it is heuristic. cmd_pack_objects, L5113 sorts candidate objects — by type, name-hash, and size, so similar filenames are adjacent in the window — then try_delta, L2802 diffs each candidate against neighbors until the delta stops improving, bounded by --depth and a max-size rule that rejects deltas larger than half the target. On write, existing deltas from source packs are copied verbatim when valid (write_reuse_object, L635), falling back to encoding from scratch in write_no_reuse_object, L516 when the reuse checks fail. The heuristics are explained further in pack-heuristics.adoc. This is why histories that look similar can pack differently: window contents and base selection differ per repository.

How a Commit Walk Actually Traverses

Every git log, rev-list, and merge-base computation funnels through one engine. setup_revisions, L3048 parses arguments like A..B into object flags; then prepare_revision_walk, L4019 takes the pending tips, sorts them by commit date, and chooses a strategy: if the request is “limited” — anything with exclusions or bounds — it runs limit_list, L1446, which pops commits in date order and, upon hitting an UNINTERESTING commit, floods that mark over its ancestors via mark_parents_uninteresting, L278. That flood is what makes git log main..feature terminate at the merge base instead of walking to the dawn of time.

Parsing each commit is parse_commit_buffer, L516: validate the tree line, collect every parent line, and attach them — with graft and shallow-clone substitutions applied where configured. The two orderings git offers fall out cleanly: date order needs nothing extra, while topological order is a post-pass, sort_in_topological_order, L938. The big optimization is the commit-graph file: parse_commit_in_graph, L1075 supplies parent lists and generation numbers straight from a binary index, without inflating or parsing a single commit object — which is exactly why large histories, like the Rust and TypeScript monorepos, stay fast to walk once the graph file is written.

From Clone to First Commit

Building git from source is pleasantly old-school, and the tree verifies it. The canonical instructions in INSTALL are simply make followed by make install — the top-level Makefile drives everything, with build knobs overridable via a config.mak. If you prefer autoconf, make configure regenerates the ./configure script from configure.ac, then ./configure --prefix=/usr && make all doc produces binaries and man pages. There is also a second build system: meson.build is present and documented in build-systems.adoc, and a profile-feedback build (make profile) exists that rebuilds git after running the test suite as training data — the INSTALL notes it buys a few percent on CPU-bound work at the cost of building twice.

You can run the freshly built git without installing: the build tree ships bin-wrappers/, and INSTALL documents prepending it to PATH. First commit is then git commit through the very code path traced above. Notably, the tree now also contains contrib/libgit-rs — early Rust bindings — showing the project slowly exposing its object database beyond C.

Honest Limits

The object model is stable but the hash beneath it is not final. The migration plan from SHA-1 lives in hash-function-transition.adoc: since v2.13.0 git ships a hardened SHA-1 (collision detection, vendored under sha1collisiondetection/), but SHA-1 remains the default algorithm, and the transition is implemented as plumbing — the compat-algo hashing visible in odb_write_object_ext, L696 — rather than a done deal. Repositories like Go that moved hosting around have felt similar storage-format transitions; git’s is still in progress.

Delta compression is also heuristic, not optimal: the window/depth bounds in try_delta, L2802 trade pack size for CPU, and the design doc admits the search is approximate. The index’s stat-based freshness means it can mark clean files dirty after timestamp churn (the racy-git problem, described in racy-git.adoc). And the ref layer is in mid-migration too: files, packed-refs, and reftable backends all coexist, selected per-repository. Finally, the commit-graph is strictly an accelerator — parse_commit_in_graph, L1075 only applies when the file exists and covers your commits; without it, walks inflate every commit object the old way.
entry.summary: How git really stores your history: content-addressed objects, the index, refs and reflogs, packfile delta compression, and commit graph walks — with line-level links into git's C source.
